EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on FM 705 between Broaddus and Bronson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe winds on this date were driven by a southeastward-moving shortwave trough that had overspread the region while a surface low over northwest Texas, an advancing cold front, and a dryline provided the focus for thunderstorm initiation. Strong daytime heating beneath steep mid-level lapse rates and a moist Gulf air mass produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE values generally ranging from 2,500 to 3,500 J/kg. To our north and west, initial storms developed as supercells capable of producing very large hail, but we anticipated rapid upscale growth into a forward-propagating mesoscale convective system (MCS) and bowing line segment by the time the system reached our CWA. The combination of abundant instability, a dry mid-level air mass, and strengthening forcing aloft favored the development of a strong cold pool, allowing the convective system to accelerate south-southeastward across South Texas. As storms merged and became increasingly outflow-dominant, widespread damaging straight-line winds produced corridors of significant wind damage as the system advanced toward the Texas Coast overnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station XLAG at Laguna Shores.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread crop damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought continued across portions of East Texas through the first three plus weeks of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. However, widespread rainfall amounts of 1.50 to 2.00+ inches fell across much of Rusk, Gregg, San Augustine, and Sabine Counties between the 19th  and 26th, resulting in a one category improvement to Moderate (D1) drought across these areas by the May 28th release of the U.S. Drought Monitor. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2.50-4+ inches across Rusk and Gregg Counties, and between 5-8+ inches across San Augustine and Sabine Counties, which was near to as much as twice the monthly normals. Thus, some improvement to pasture greenup, stock pond levels, and streamflows across area rivers, bayous, and creeks were observed by month's end. ||Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana. Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and a dryline allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon of the 31st. Thunderstorms initially developed along this dryline from the northern Rolling Plains into the southern South Plains. The thunderstorms gradually grew upscale into a broken, slow moving line that persisted over the central Rolling Plains into the south-central South Plains through the evening hours. These slow moving thunderstorms primarily produced torrential rainfall but also large hail and damaging wind gusts. Excessive runoff from the prolonged heavy rain flooded fields and inundated area roadways. Some of the heaviest rainfall was along US Highway 87 north of Tahoka in Lynn County. Water over the roadway and a water rescue prompted the closure of the highway. Several additional vehicles became flooded out along US Highway 87. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 west of Post (Garza County) and in northwestern Lubbock (Lubbock County). As storms decreased in intensity late in the evening, a couple of wake lows formed producing severe wind gusts near Slaton (Lubbock County) and Paducah (Cottle County).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued into April as the area still lacked any measurable precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured about one third of an inch of rain, with some localized spots up to one half of an inch. However, Dallam County ended the month about 0.8-1.2 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 2.5 inches below normal in the western part of the county to near 3 inches below normal in the eastern part. The drought worsened through the month, with northern parts of Dallam County creeping into Extreme Drought (D3).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of water covering the road, making the roadway impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought continued across portions of Deep East Texas through the first week of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. However, widespread rainfall amounts of 1.50 to 2.00+ inches fell across much of Cherokee, Nacogdoches, and Angelina Counties during the last few days of April into the first week of May, resulting in a one category improvement to Moderate (D1) drought across these areas by the May 7th release of the U.S. Drought Monitor. Timely near to above normal rainfall continued across these areas through the remainder of May, with monthly rainfall totals ranging from 3-6+ inches, near to slightly above the monthly normals. Thus, some improvement to pasture greenup, stock pond levels, and streamflows across area rivers, bayous, and creeks were observed, especially as the additional timely rains fell through the remainder of the month.

Rainfall was above normal across the area in May. The Hill Country, Coastal Plains, and Winter Garden areas received up to three times normal rain. This resulted in improvement or maintenance of the drought. Dimmit, Medina, and Travis Counties all improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Hays County remained in D3. Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 20.6 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were still below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 5.7 feet but was 11.1 feet below normal. Canyon Lake remained the same as in April and was 22.3 feet below normal. Lake Amistad dropped 0.7 feet and was 69.8 feet below normal. Medina Lake rose 0.3 feet but was still 87.1 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) to much below (<10%) normal on the Medina and Blanco Rivers; below normal on the lower Colorado River; and below normal to normal (25%-75%) on the lower Guadalupe and San Marcos Rivers. All other rivers were normal to much above normal (90%-95%).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable air mass was in place across South Texas, with surface dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s and strong daytime heating producing moderate to strong instability. Sea-breeze boundaries along the Middle Texas Coast served as a focus for thunderstorm development during the afternoon. While upper-level winds were relatively weak, sufficient instability and moderate deep-layer shear supported organized convection capable of producing damaging wind gusts. A compact MCS developed near Corpus Christi and moved along the coast, where a favorable thermodynamic environment allowed it to intensify. The storm complex produced severe wind gusts, including measured gusts of 53-59 kt in Corpus Christi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Column anchorage failed on metal building system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few short lived thunderstorms formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle on the evening of May 13th. One of these storms was exiting Gray County as it was dissipating and the environment left behind helped cause a heat burst in Gray County, which led to gusts around 60 mph. The next day, May 14th, scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region. Finally, on the evening of the 15th, showers and thunderstorms developed over the northwest combined Panhandles. These storms also produced severe wind gusts across portions of the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Repeated rounds of rainfall throughout May significantly improved drought conditions across South Texas and the Coastal Bend. Early-month rainfall totals generally ranged from 2 to 6 inches along the Coastal Bend and 1 to 10 inches across South Texas, with additional rainfall continuing through mid-May. Several storms produced strong winds, hail, and tornado warnings, resulting in localized damage. A more significant rainfall event occurred during the last week of May, when multiple storm systems produced widespread totals of 1 to 12 inches, with localized amounts exceeding 5 inches along portions of the Coastal Bend. The heavy rainfall led to localized creek flooding and more widespread flooding in portions of Refugio County. By month's end, topsoil and subsoil moisture had improved from short to surplus in many locations, substantially alleviating drought impacts and improving rangeland, pasture, and water availability across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to widespread D2.

The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.

Repeated rounds of rainfall throughout May significantly improved drought conditions across South Texas and the Coastal Bend. Early-month rainfall totals generally ranged from 2 to 6 inches along the Coastal Bend and 1 to 10 inches across South Texas, with additional rainfall continuing through mid-May. Several storms produced strong winds, hail, and tornado warnings, resulting in localized damage. A more significant rainfall event occurred during the last week of May, when multiple storm systems produced widespread totals of 1 to 12 inches, with localized amounts exceeding 5 inches along portions of the Coastal Bend. The heavy rainfall led to localized creek flooding and more widespread flooding in portions of Refugio County. By month's end, topsoil and subsoil moisture had improved from short to surplus in many locations, substantially alleviating drought impacts and improving rangeland, pasture, and water availability across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D1 by 5/26, ending inclusion in Storm Data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued into April as the area still lacked any measurable precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured about one half of an inch of rain, with some localized spots up to 1.5 inches. However, Sherman County ended the month about 0.2-0.8 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 2.5 to 3 inches below normal. The bulk of the county remained in D2 drought through the month but far northern parts of Sherman County creeped into Extreme Drought (D3) near the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of minor weather disturbances moved through the region from April 9th through the 11th. These combined with increased moisture to bring showers and storms to the region. With enough wind shear available in the atmosphere, some of these storms brought severe wind gusts to the region. Dry and windy conditions were in place on April 9th and that helped drive the spread of a wildfire known as The Smooth Eddy Incident which was over 500 acres. Additionally, the Purple Monster Wildfire would be sparked due to dry lightning in Oldham County on the evening of April 9th. That fire would go on to burn 1,911 acres.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

A few short lived thunderstorms formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle on the evening of May 13th. One of these storms was exiting Gray County as it was dissipating and the environment left behind helped cause a heat burst in Gray County, which led to gusts around 60 mph. The next day, May 14th, scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region. Finally, on the evening of the 15th, showers and thunderstorms developed over the northwest combined Panhandles. These storms also produced severe wind gusts across portions of the area.

A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down at the 2500 Block of FM 1519 southeast of Leesburg.

Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms were initially transient and struggled to become organized due to a lack of deep layer shear across the region. However, numerous outflow boundary formed which initiated new convection and were able to take advantage of a moist and unstable atmosphere. Hail as large as tennis balls were observed in Hale County. The numerous outflow boundaries created enough shear to generate several landspout tornadoes across the area. None of the many landspout tornadoes caused any known damage. Additionally, merging storms in southeastern Hale County produced torrential rainfall which led to flash flooding of roads and fields north of Petersburg.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several storm chasers reported a swath of hail northwest of Petersburg. Hail ranged in size from half dollars to just over two inches in diameter. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 14th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Furthermore, dry lightning initiated a wildfire just west of Matador. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged hot and dry period was set up for the Panhandles in mid May.  And with the lack of significant rainfall to help transition the grasses from cured to green, the fuels were well above the 90th percentile in dryness.  While it's not uncommon for a high based storm or two to occur west of the dryline and create dry thunderstorms, on May 14th it was certainly more scattered to nearly widespread storms that occurred.  Several lightning ignitions occurred, and given that the storms had severe dry microbursts associated, the fires that ignited would spread quickly.  Thereafter the Panhandles would go through several consecutive days of critical to extremely critical conditions.  And the issues of any new starts, as well as active fires that ignited on May 14th would take another run were of high concern.  Overall 20 wildfires ranging from over 34,000 acres to some as small as a few acres would ignite in the TX/OK Panhandle between the 14th and the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Chocolate Chip Fire ignited on the morning of Friday the 15th about 17 miles southwest of Canyon, TX.  The winds caused this fire within just hours of igniting to expand to over 10,000 acres moving so fast it managed to jump interstate 27.  By Friday afternoon it merged with the Hunggate Fire.  At this point since it is part of the Hunggate fire it's 95 percent contained.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation and expansion of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D3 drought.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: On March 10th, a high based thunderstorm with dry lightning ignited a wildfire in far southwest Moore County. The fire, which would be named Yellow Fire, sparked around 6:30pm and occurred near the border of Moore, Oldham and Hartley counties. Gusty, erratic winds occurred at the Boys Ranch mesonet around that time, and while relative humidity values were around 20%, the winds and the critically dry fuels allowed for rapid wildfire growth. The wildfire was estimated to have burned 14,374 acres and was contained on March 13th. East and westbound SH 354 was temporarily closed from US Highway 385 to US Highway 87 from March 10th through early on the 11th. Additional roads also experienced at least temporary closures such as RM 1061 at FM 281 and Highway 385. There was also a voluntary evacuation of Valley de Oro and an evacuation of the Boys Ranch community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation and expansion of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter size hail reported between the Alba and Golden communities.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very isolated rain events brought some moisture to the eastern Panhandles during the month. However, this did not put a dent in the 120 departure from normal with values staying 2 to 4 below normal. Mites were appearing on stressed winter wheat crop and wildfires became an increasing concern across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate Drought (D1) conditions persisted in the NW TX Panhandle until the third week of March. At that point, the drought intensified, with Dallam, Hartley, Sherman, and Moore Counties all escalating to Severe Drought (D2). This transition was marked by an additional 1 to 2 being added to the existing 120-day precipitation deficit. Furthermore, the severity of the drought's impact on winter crops was worsened by record monthly maximum temperatures recorded during the month.

Strong winds over very dry topsoil also led to sporadic reductions in visibility (and vehicle incidents) due to blowing dust. High Wind events included in this episode capture the first, last and highest magnitude wind gust in a particular zone/county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Seymour (SEYM) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The lack of rainfall during winter 2025/2026 resulted in a continuation of drought conditions across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to begin March. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported at the intersection of H.G. Mosley Parkway and Bill Owens Parkway in Longview.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across Gregg, Smith, and Upshur Counties in East Texas by late March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged between 2-4 inches, which was a continuation of below normal rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) drought expanded across more of East Texas by the end of the month.

South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The lack of rainfall during winter 2025/2026 resulted in a continuation of drought conditions across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to begin March. D2 (Severe Drought) to D3 (Extreme Drought) was common to start March, with a small area of Exceptional Drought (D4) across the Brush Country.  Additionally, the area saw deepening/expansion of these categories and the month we on. From the last week in February to the first week of March, D4 (Exceptional Drought) increased across 8% of the area from 18% to 26%, and the combination of D2 to D4 increased from 91 to 97% of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Through March 10, D2 (Severe Drought) was present over all of the Kenedy County barrier island with the exception of the extreme northeastern section. D2 conditions would overspread that northeast sliver between March 17 and 23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms extended from Southeast Oklahoma down across Central Texas late in the evening on March 10th and into the early morning on March 11th, with the most organized threat area over Northeast Texas into Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Effective storm-relative helicity ahead of the prominent line of thunderstorms was quite favorable for low-level rotation, and instability was rather strong as well. As a result, severe thunderstorms produced some damaging wind gusts in parts of Deep East Texas during the early morning hours on March 11th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Small softwood tree trunk snapped and downed across FM Road 1818 south of U.S. Highway 69 and west of Zavalla.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed in advance of a cold front on the morning of March 7th from eastern Oklahoma into western Arkansas. Wind profiles were quite favorable for organized thunderstorms, with moderate deep-layer shear and effective storm-relative helicity near/above 250 m2/s2. Further analysis also indicated a modest increase in MLCAPE overnight into the early morning hours in the pre-frontal warm air regime, as rich low-level moisture was transported into the region from the southwest. Farther south, storms also increased in coverage and intensity across Northeast Texas, within the zone of deep and rich low-level moisture. This led to some intensification of convection prior to the arrival of the approaching cold front, with one thunderstorm producing a tornado near the Prospect community in central Marion County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Early on the morning of March 7th, a severe thunderstorm produced an EF2 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 115 mph near the community of Prospect in Northern Marion County, Texas. The tornado initially touched down just west of U.S. Highway 59 where multiple snapped trunks of hardwood trees were noted. As the tornado continued east, it heavily damaged several structures. A residential home west of the highway was damaged by a fallen tree. Next to the home, a barn was completely destroyed, with only the wooden frame remaining. Debris from the barn along with the barn's contents were strewn across the front yard and into the highway median and onto the northbound side of the highway. Just to the east of U.S. Highway 59, another residential home experienced significant damage after being shifted feet away from its foundation. Several large hardwood trees were also uprooted and fell onto a nearby shed. Just north of this home, another home experienced tornado damage. In the backyard of this home, a small shed was completely destroyed, with contents strewn across the yard, along with damage to vehicles. At this residence, a camper was tossed and rolled into another nearby shed, where multiple occupants were thrown about and injured. The tornado continued east/northeast, snapping and uprooting numerous trees before moving into additional residential areas on East Prospect Road. Here, additional damage to several roofs was noted, sheds and barns experienced significant damage, along with major hardwood tree snaps and downed power lines. The tornado weakened as it moved northeast away from East Prospect Road and crossed Scotts Bayou. Some tree damage was found along Hall Road before the tornado then lifted as it moved east along East CC Road and toward the town of Lodi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation and expansion of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed on a power line along County Road 432 just east of the Anthony Harbor community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense cold front, associated with a deepening midlatitude cyclone across the central CONUS, fostered a non-convective wind and wildfire episode across Oklahoma and western-north Texas during the morning into early evening of the 15th. Strong winds over very dry topsoil also led to sporadic reductions in visibility (and vehicle incidents) due to blowing dust. High Wind events included in this episode capture the first, last and highest magnitude wind gust in a particular zone/county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of East Texas through roughly the first half of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged between 2-4 inches, which was a continuation of below normal rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. However, widespread wetting rains of 1-3+ inches fell across much of Deep East Texas on March 11th, resulting in improvement to moderate drought (D1) in the March 19th issuance of the U.S. Drought Monitor.
Thunderstorms developed along a cold front and one of these storms produced large hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to just D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball size hail reported in the Reklaw community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. High precipitable water (PWAT) values of 1.7+ inches within the unstable environment supported strong downdrafts capable of isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of East Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree downed at the corner of Baylor Drive and Karen Drive in Tyler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As developing Tropical Storm Arthur moved along the middle Texas coast (June 17) and as a degenerated low pressure system along the Louisiana Coast (June 18), very hot air descended on the southern tip of Texas, with record extreme heat index, or feels-like, temperatures for the entire region on the 18th.  The high heat index values held on into June 19th, before unsettled weather brought slightly lower temperatures and pockets of rain by the 20th, which ended the short but brutal window of extreme heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures near or just above 100 degrees and high humidity, a remnant of rainfall associated with tropical moisture as Tropical Storm Arthur began to form, created heat index values between 111 and 113, with a peak of 114, in southern Hidalgo County (McAllen Miller Int'l Airport).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. High precipitable water (PWAT) values of 1.7+ inches within the unstable environment supported strong downdrafts capable of isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of East Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in Lindale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding. 5.11 inches of rain was measured in Marshall in Central Harrison County from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several cars were stalled in high water on King Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees downed across Bowie County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A repeating band of slow-moving showers and thunderstorms over the Weslaco/Donna area during the early to mid morning of June 15th produced areas of notable flash flooding.  Up to 7 inches of rain fell in a little more than two hours, leaving some streets with up to three feet of water depth and water into several properties. Another round of thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon across Starr and Jim Hogg County, with urban flooding across portions of Rio Grande City based on an estimated 3-5 of rainfall there.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Torrential rainfall the began just before the morning commute would soon add up to notable flash flooding across Weslaco, parts of Mercedes, and extending westward to the east side of Donna and southward to near US 281 (Progreso). Rainfall totals of near 7 inches were recorded along IH-2 near the Mid-Valley Airport, in just over two hours. Flash flooding included numerous streets, including the frontage road, with 2-3 feet of water as well as several properties with water incursion into them. Some of the reports included:|*Numerous social media reports and news media coverage of flooding along the I-2 frontage road in Weslaco near North Republic St and North Texas Blvd.|*The IH-2 frontage road was closed (eastbound) between Westgate and Texas Boulevard (Exits 157 to 155).  |*A city disaster declaration was issued by the Mayor of Weslaco due to the extensive nature of the flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across much of Northeast Texas through the month of June, although some improvement to drought was observed as widespread 3-8+ inches of rain fell across these areas, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 12 inches falling across much of Red River and Western Bowie Counties. While some of the rain was excessive and resulted in flash flooding at times, improvement to soil moisture as well as streamflow was observed across much of Northeast Texas, with ag producers reporting improvement to stock pond levels and greenup of pastures. Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A car was stranded in high water on FM Road 248 between Kildare and Bivins. A high water rescue was needed to rescue the stranded driver.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley bordering Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Northeast Texas, and into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours of June 19th, with a warm, very moist and unstable air mass present across East Texas along and south of the front. An upper level disturbance traversed atop the front during the morning and early afternoon hours, enhancing large scale forcing for the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along and south of the front. Given the very moist air mass in place, these storms were very efficient rainfall producers, with widespread rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling over Central and Northern Red River and Bowie Counties in Northeast Texas. These excessive rainfall amounts in a short period of time resulted in reports of flash flooding across these areas, particularly in the Detroit and Dekalb areas with multiple roads flooded and water entering homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water entered several homes and buildings in Detroit. Report from mPING.

A broad area of mostly elevated strong to severe thunderstorms developed and shifted southward across Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex along an advancing cold front throughout the day on April 29th. Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. As a result, numerous reports of large hail were recorded across parts of East Texas along with an isolated report of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported along Highway 103 West near Lufkin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.
Severe to extreme drought conditions covered much of East Texas and eastern Central Texas throughout the month of April 2026, though minor improvements occurred during the latter half of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions covered Robertson County for all of April 2026, along with a few instances of Extreme Drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree branches were snapped near the intersection of Highway 155 and West Grande Boulevard, causing minor damage to a nearby building.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued into April as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured around 0.10 inches of rain but the far northwest part of the county may have gotten some precipitation and amounts of 0.8 to near 1 inch was measured. However, Hutchinson County ended the month about one half of an inch to 1.8 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was all below normal around 2.5 inches in the far northwest to 3.8 inches across much of the county. The county remained in D2 drought through about middle to end of the month when the bulk of the county deteriorated to Extreme Drought (D3).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Northeast Texas during the evening with reports of widespread damaging wind gusts along with a handful of large hail reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from dime to half dollar size reported in the Judson community near the intersection of U.S. Highway 259 and FM Road 1844.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.
Severe to extreme drought conditions covered much of East Texas and eastern Central Texas throughout the month of April 2026, though minor improvements occurred during the latter half of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Northeast Texas during the evening with reports of widespread damaging wind gusts along with a handful of large hail reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from pea to quarter size covered the ground on the south side of Tyler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Northeast Texas during the evening with reports of widespread damaging wind gusts along with a handful of large hail reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees uprooted along FM Road 127 between FM Road 21 in Monticello.

Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southeast portion of Ochiltree County was in Moderate Drought (D1) to start April while the remainder of the county was in Severe Drought (D2). By the middle of the month, the entire county was in Severe Drought, with some Extreme Drought (D3) creeping into the far northern and far southern portions of the county by mid to late April. This worsening drought was due to the lack of continuous, significant rainfall. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county but amounts were sparse. In total, the county measured 0.1 to 0.4 inches of rain. Ochiltree County ended the month about 1.4-1.7 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 3.5-4.2 inches below normal.

Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As developing Tropical Storm Arthur moved along the middle Texas coast (June 17) and as a degenerated low pressure system along the Louisiana Coast (June 18), very hot air descended on the southern tip of Texas, with record extreme heat index, or feels-like, temperatures for the entire region on the 18th.  The high heat index values held on into June 19th, before unsettled weather brought slightly lower temperatures and pockets of rain by the 20th, which ended the short but brutal window of extreme heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures near of just above 100 degrees and high humidity, a remnant of rainfall associated with tropical moisture as Tropical Storm Arthur began to form, created heat index values estimated to be between 111 and 114, with a peak of 115, in inland Willacy County.  Observed data from Valley International Airport (Harlingen, about 8 miles south of the county line) and Brooks County Airport (near Falfurrias) were used as proxy data for this area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As developing Tropical Storm Arthur moved along the middle Texas coast (June 17) and as a degenerated low pressure system along the Louisiana Coast (June 18), very hot air descended on the southern tip of Texas, with record extreme heat index, or feels-like, temperatures for the entire region on the 18th.  The high heat index values held on into June 19th, before unsettled weather brought slightly lower temperatures and pockets of rain by the 20th, which ended the short but brutal window of extreme heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures reaching to or just below 100 degrees, combined with high humidity left behind from earlier week rainfall, allowed heat index to rise to above 111 by early afternoon in Brownsville and Harlingen, peaking just below 120 (119.7) in Brownsville at 3:53 PM CDT, and at 111 at Harlingen/Valley Airport at 1:52 PM CDT. The general range was 111 to 114 degrees; the 119.7 value was just for a short while at Brownsville/South Padre Int'l Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.
We had a few wildfires that occurred in early April.  A couple in Hutchinson County (North and South Twin), and another Fire in Potter County (Meadow View).  The fires ranged from 365-1262 acres.
